#### Chapter 1

##### 1: Slippery Roof

So few controlled so many but Vanilan was one of another few; the clever and free. The world was run on a promise kept by a few to the many that they had no intention of keeping. \
\
The many were fed lies about how things were supposed to be; what was true and what was inconceivable. \
\
The many were hoodwinked to believe that they had magic pieces of paper in their pockets that were valuable. These paper's didn't make electricity. They didn't heal wounds on their own. The newer, plastic pieces didn't even produce flame like the old paper ones. They just shrivelled and melted. \
\
The power of these plastic pieces was what people believed them to be worth. People, like they usually do, let other people tell them what to believe. They believed that the pieces were worth enough to exchange for goods, services, and what have you. If people in power decided tomorrow that the bills were worth nothing, then that would be true. People would be left holding worthless artefacts of a foolish time, while other people held everything. That day was coming and it was closer than almost everyone thought it was. Vanilan was on the right side of the almost.\
\
It wasn't always like this. The notes used to be weighed against something of actual value. That value was gold. Why gold? Gold didn't age. It stayed shiny and didn't decompose. The earliest gold coins have been found in Asia Minor, the ancient land forming modern day Turkey, dating back 600 years before the supposed birth of Jesus. Since then, the exchange of gold (and silver which is equally indestructible) helped propel humanity to the heights it's reached today. \
\
Gold was hard to carry around everywhere, and hide in your pants too. People started writing notes that promised redemption for real gold to buyers to help ease trade and commerce. That's how the plastic notes in people's pockets started. They were IOUs for shiny bullion.\
\
However, at a certain point people thought it would be good to go a step further and detach the promise of gold in exchange. They convinced the masses that the paper would hold value simply by the promise of men in power.\
\
Much smaller promises were broken every day. Caesar promised Rome he wouldn't cross the Rubicon. Hitler promised Britain he wouldn't invade Czechoslovakia.\
\
All it would take for things to go badly was a broken promise. That's why Vanilan always promoted gold. No matter rupees, rubles, dinars dollars, they all had a tendency to come and go with regimes, wars and empires. But gold. Gold stayed the same. Gold and silver held intrinsic value that could not be changed. If gold ever disappeared, society would disappear. We could have started the whole affair with coconut shells, but there wass a reason we chose gold, and a reason we would have to go back to it at one point or another. Vanilan knew that point would be soon.\
\
Once the secret society came out of the shadows, it was those who had assets of real value that would prevail. While everyone else was busy sending friend requests and clubbing downtown, Vanilan was preparing for the new world order.\
\
He currently held paper gold', online commodity purchases redeemable for physical gold on demand. The redeemable part was critical. He reckoned to at least have a year before the monetary system imploded. That was enough time for to liquidate and line his basement walls with the real stuff. While it may have appeared contradictory, he needed to work within the system to escape it.\
\
It was important not to have any distractions. He had traded in all of his game systems and peddle bike for a new office chair and investment capital. His bedroom was my office, thus saving on rent. His diet consisted of snacking on washed kale and apple slices in order to detox from processed sugar and fat. He occasionally splurged in Doritos when the munchies got to him. He liked to trade using a comfy wardrobe. That could be as simple as a hoodie with no undershirt and sweatpants. It was important to be comfortable when trading for long periods of time.\
\
He traded using a desk set up that included 3 monitors. His laptop screen was one of them, where he did most of his work. He also had a flatscreen and one of those big old cube shaped monitors from the early 2000s. That way we could see multiple things at once. He would have one screen glued to the spot prices of all his current trades: gold, silver, key currency pairs and a few companies. The cubed monitor was set up to watch the news. A good trader kept his fingers to the pulse of global events at all times.\
\
Right then it was tuned into a vacant mic on a public access livestream; awaiting the spokesman of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. He was watching the news awaiting an announcement on interest rates. If the rates were cut, it would mean more people would spend and thus less incentive to buy investments. Vanilan was sure that rates would be hiked in a turn of recent momentum. This meant that people would shift their behaviour back to saving and thus the price of gold would rise significantly. He only had $100 invested in this move, but he had to start somewhere. If things went great he could make 50% return, and then shift $150 to another opportunity. It was raining outside. There was no excuse but to hustle.\
\
The phone rang. It was Logic calling.\
\
"Yeah," said Vanilan.\
\
"What's on TV?" said Logic. \
\
There was some ignorant rap thumping in the background on Logic's end.\
\
"Interest rate hike in New Zealand about to spike the price of AU," said Vanilan.\
\
He eyed the microphone again as it seems like people were filing into the press room.\
\
"Just call it gold. You sound like a douche," said Logic. \
\
Vanilan heard a turn signal starting clicking on the other end. He was in a car.\
\
"What are you doing?" said Vanilan.\
\
"On my way to a hotel party. Got bitches lined up," said Logic.\
\
"Cool," said Vanilan. \
\
He was happy not be caught up in all that noise, especially with a likely spike looming.\
\
"I can't go back home or else I can't come back out. Hold something for me," said Logic.\
\
"Yeah no worries," said Vanilan. \
\
He was clicking through some candle charts now.\
\
"Alright then, come outside," said Logic.\
\
"Wait, you're here right now?" said Vanilan. \
\
Things had gotten real.\
\
"My boy is driving me there. We're outside. Can you hurry up?" said Logic.\
\
"Which boy?" said Vanilan.\
\
"It's Caveman. The guy with the overbite." said Logic.\
\
"Fuck you," said a voice.\
\
Vanilan got up from the desk and looked out the window. A blue Camry was parked at the end of the driveway. Through the sheet of rain two cigarette ends glowed and then faded from inside the windshield.\
\
"Oh, 
that 
guy," said Vanilan.\
\
"Come outside," said Logic.\
\
"Nah, it's too late. If you my bell my mom's gonna open the door," said Vanilan.\
\
Suits were assembling behind the microphone. A few flashes went off.\
\
"It's me. And I'm giving you a backpack." Logic was annoyed.\
\
"It's midnight. She'll open it," said Vanilan.\
\
"Guy, I can't take it to the party. It's two pounds and I already got a half-O in my socks. Break some off if you want," said Logic.\
\
Vanilan lifted the window. The rain was slow enough to hear individual rain drops. It was a great night to get blazed in the upstairs bathroom.\
\
"Aim it at my window, but a little bit short. I'll grab it when it lands on the roof."\
\
"You mean, like, throw it?" asked Logic. He was already getting out of the car.\
\
"I've done it before. As long as it's flat it'll stick until I can grab it." said Vanilan.\
\
"Alright. It's on the way up," said Logic.\
\
The backpack flew funny, like those balls that people played badminton with. It landed flat on the sloped roof midway between the eavestrough and the bedroom window.\
\
"Got it," said Vanilan. He hung up.\
\
Logic was jogging back to the passenger side when Vanilan leans his torso outside with an open palm reaching for the closest handle. He was about a foot short. If he leaned any further his feet would lift off the ground and that would be scary. He came back inside as the car swerved off. He would have to climb out to get it. He angled himself sidways to the window so he could get his first foot outdoors.\

\
"The Reserve Bank is currently prepared to lower the prime interest rate to 0.7%."
\
\
Shit.\
\
When he bent his torso forward the excess fat on his belly compressed to form a less squishy gut. If he had been wearing belted jeans instead of his sweatpants, it would have been quite restricting to move around like this.Vanilan stuck a leg out of the window. As he shifted his weight outside his heel shifted and his pelvis fell hit the sill, two inches shy of his balls. The rain had slickened the shingles. The backpack slipped backwards succumbing to the same forces. He reached an arm for it while trying to get himself out of the splits. He bent his leg in and pillared his weigh on a knee. His anchor hand gripped the drywall above the window's interior. He watched as the backpack slipped further back and over the edge. Over the rain he heard it slap to a stop onto the front porch below.\
\
The gold rush had just suffered a major setback.\

##### 2: Get A Job

They thought Logic was a saint because Vanilan made him look like one. It was convenient when he needed to throw someones name out to make them calm down when he went out at night, but fucking annoying in times like this. In fact, this was a really fucking annoying circumstance.\

Dad picked up a brick of weed and started turning it over in his hands. He held it up towards the ceiling light while he did it like a jeweller checking diamonds. Dad looked surprised by that revelation. He always wore his work clothes at home so he carried sawdust with him everywhere. It was a ballsy act by Mom because if any of those plates broke she would've held a day of mourning for it.\

 Dad stirred with a jolt, like he'd nodded off for a second. He had a tendency to do that. Vanilan didn't know how he got through work because he was perpetually tired. He'd fallen asleep while driving up to Wasaga when Vanilan was 14. That was probably the only time Vanilan had ever hit his dad.\

how do they have the news if it's only 9 AM?'\

##### 4: Inspection

A friend of Vanilan's from high school ran a car repair shop now. His name was Chuck Yeager, like the astronaut. The shop was on off Highway 27, a large industrial block down from Uncle Amaran's favourite massage parlour. \

There were 6 folding chairs and a wooden desk for actual reception duties. The girl sitting there could've been Chuck's sister but she was in ninth grade when Vanilan saw her last. He asked for Chuck by name. She didn't recognize Vanilan, and told him to bring in car around back and wait for the left bay door to open. \
\
There were cars in varying degrees of disassembly lined the back of the garage. To their rear was a fence leading to green space where power lines ran up the spine of Rexdale. A few errand car parts had been chucked over by whoever.\

Chuck put some distance between them and made himself busy.\
\
"Yeah. I'm the co-owner. We opened up last fall. Where's Logic at?" said Chuck.\
\
"Don't know. I'm getting busy with my business game too. Trading stocks and gold. Making a killing," said Vanilan.\
\
He stopped slouching. He had to think about slouching in order not to do it. If he was thinking about slouching he couldn't think about other stuff, more important stuff.\
\
"Oh, good for you brother. Tell Logic I said what's cracking.' So, this is just a tune up, or, what exactly?" said Chuck.\
\
"Uh, I'm trying to get approved for Jockey," said Vanilan.\
\
He made to hand Chuck the forms he'd been pinching.\
\
"I'll take that at the end. Greasy, remember. You too? Tough Guy came through last week and that dude who used to wear those hitched up pants. Him too, like, last month," said Chuck.\
\
Vanilan wasn't ever close to as basic as those guys. He was going to freak this Jockey thing in a revolutionary way.\
\
Chuck was holding the hoist controls now. The suspension adjusted to the slightly shifting weight as the car rose 10 feet into the air.\
\
"Yeah it's a good way to diversify revenue streams. I get tired of making money sitting in front of a computer all day. This way I can get out and get in touch with the greater universe. I'm mostly going to cater to the downtown investor crowd," said Vanilan.\
\
Chuck set the controls aside and eyed Vanilan up and down.\
\
"You may want to dress a bit sharper if you want to drive those kinds of guys around guy," said Chuck.\
\
He stepped under the car and craned his neck upwards. He started at the tailpipe and worked his way forward.\
\
Vanilan's face felt hot now. The heat from the previously running car must have been making it's way to him.\
\
"Get maybe a few white dress shirts and black ties. Tough Guy keeps things like gum and chips in his cup holders. That might impress people. If you show up dressed like that, I mean it's OK for the hood and all, but rich people might complain," said Chuck.\
\
Vanilan walked towards the car to get a good look at a fresh side of it. He tried to naem as many parts as he could. Muffler. Gas Tank. Engine.\
\
"Yeah I may have to break out the suits. You know how people in the hood get if you start flashing your cash," said Vanilan.\
\
"Careful, even newer cars can leak a bit of oil here and there," said Chuck.\
\
Vanilan heeded the caution and stepped back\
\
"I wouldn't worry about a suit jacket. You're just going to sweat sitting in a car all day," said Chuck.\
\
"\
\
"This car looks OK to..."\
\
"It's been in an accident. The car," interrupted Vanilan.\
\
"An accident?"\
\
"Yeah the bumper fell off. My dad wasn't looking and a guy came at him from the side at a stop sign."\
\
"OK. I don't know then."\
\
"Come on, you said you were gonna hook it up," said Vanilan.\
\
Chuck did a few cirles underneath vehicle and his flashlights's light darted around the wrinkles of the underbelly.\
\
"There's a bit of trauma, now that I know what I'm looking for," said Chuck.\
\
"Really? Is it a big deal?" said Vanilan.\
\
Chuck assessed the situation a for a bit longer. He breathed deeply before speaking again.\
\
"I'm going to have to put in a new defibrillator," said Chuck. \
\
He didn't look back at Vanilan to deliver the prognosis.\
\
"How much will that cost?" said Vanilan.\
\
Chuck thought about it.\
\
"I think I've got a used one in stock. It works just fine. If you're OK with that I can give it away for only $200."\
\
That was worth fifth of an ounce of gold.\
\
"Yeah, that's no problem," said Vanilan.\
\
Chuck snapped the flashlight off and came back out. \
\
"Don't worry. I'll make it look like nothing happened. No other mechanic will even be able to tell," said Chuck.\
\
"Thanks a lot man," said Vanilan.\
\
"Good luck with the Jockey thing. If you ever need a quick fix come right back. Here, take some cards for people." Chuck reached in his back pocket for some business cards and handed them to Vanilan.\
\
"Is Logic coming by at all?" said Chuck.\
\
"Nah, don't know where he is," said Vanilan.\
\
"There's a Tim Hortons, KFC and Afghan place on the other side of the street. You can also chill in the waiting toom but we only have a water cooler and no wifi. Come back in 2 hours and it'll be wrapped up," Chuck shouted from the tool bench where he'd gone to wipe his hands.\
\
"Alright."\
\
He resolved to head across for Tims. He had change for a muffin and french vanilla. He could get some trading done. He hoped they'd having charging ports. His laptop was at 28% when he left home. Home much more trading would $200 have bought?\
\
He stopped near the bay doors and turned around.\
\
"You take credit cards right?"\
\
Chuck was pouring himself some coffee from a thermos.\
\
"$2 surcharge."

#### Chapter 2

##### 5: Barf

Kiyosaki's Rich Dad Poor Dad' was a fascinating book. Vanilan had paid good money to see the man himself when he came through Toronto in January. It was crazy how the universe just aligned for him. He had started reading about him online and then found a PDF of his book online. He was through the first 20 pages when one day he found out about the appearance. He bought a copy in the Sheraton lobby so he could get it signed. It was his first autograph and it made him happy. He never was into sports and thus didn;t hae the usual jersey or basebal or other bullshit with a scribble on it. Sports were a distraction for the dumb, deaf and blind to forget about their eventual demise.\
\
Mr. Kiyosaki makes a point of stating that real wealth comes when your monthly income from investments an sustain your monthly expense without you having to work. Vanilan was daydreaming about how that would be when his phone vibrated on the console. Jockey's logo, a horseman jumped over a fence, had pushed into his top left display.\
\
It was his first fare. He was looking at a picture of, an older lady? It was pixelated and looked to be the same quality as the 10 MB porn clip he'd first downloaded off Limewire. Her name was Alice and he hoped she wasn't made of Lego.\
\
Vanilan put the book away and pulled out of the mall parking lot.\
\
When he got to Stove Top there were a couple of couchs tossed in front of the dumptser. Stove Top was designed to be driven in to and driven out of on the other end of the block. It was tough for police to get in and out rapidly without bikes. His grade 1 home room teacher had taught him that the affordable housing had orignally been built for military. The open courtyard with minimal road exits, and the modern neighbourhood demographics, now made it make sense to lock his doors before turning in.\
\
\
"So how's your day going?" said Vanilan.\
\
He smiled at Alice through the rear view mirror.\
\
She was looking ahead but turned her gaze out of the side window. She didn't respond.
